client: I've been really struggling lately trying to keep everything together while my partner is away on a work trip. Between putting in full days at the marketing firm and then coming home to take care of two young kids on my own, I'm just completely exhausted all the time. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the situation is what it is and it's not like therapy can make my partner come home sooner.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — managing work, parenting solo, and running on empty — and it makes complete sense that you'd feel drained and even a little skeptical about whether talking can help. You're right that therapy can't change the external situation, but what it *can* do is help you find ways to feel less overwhelmed within it, and maybe ease some of the pressure you're putting on yourself to hold everything together perfectly. What does "keeping everything together" look like to you — what would it mean if something slipped a little?

client: Honestly, "keeping everything together" means the kids are fed, bathed, and in bed on time, the house isn't a total disaster, and I show up to work not looking like a complete mess. If something slipped, I think I'd feel like I was failing them — like I'm not enough on my own without my partner there. And that thought honestly terrifies me, because what does it say about me as a parent if I can't handle two weeks without falling apart?
therapist: That fear of "not being enough" is such a painful thought to carry, especially when you're already working so hard just to meet each day's demands. It's worth gently noticing that you've described feeding, bathing, and getting two kids to bed while holding down a full-time job — that's actually a lot of evidence that you *are* managing, even if it doesn't feel that way from the inside. What do you think it would take for you to see that same situation through the eyes of a close friend — would they see someone failing, or someone doing something really difficult?

client: I mean, logically I know a friend would probably tell me I'm doing a good job and that it's okay to struggle. But when I try to actually picture that, it just feels kind of hollow, like I'm trying to convince myself of something I don't really believe. I think part of the problem is that I hold myself to a completely different standard than I would hold anyone else, and I'm not sure just thinking about a friend's perspective is enough to change that.
therapist: That insight — noticing that you hold yourself to a completely different standard than you'd hold anyone else — is actually a really important and honest observation, and it takes real self-awareness to see that. The hollowness you're feeling makes sense, because just *thinking* a kinder thought doesn't automatically make you *believe* it, and CBT isn't about forcing yourself to feel something you don't. I'm curious — where do you think that harsher standard for yourself originally came from, and has it always shown up in parenting, or is this something you recognize in other areas of your life too?

client: Honestly, it shows up everywhere — at work I'm always convinced I'm one mistake away from people realizing I'm not as capable as they think, and even in my marriage I sometimes feel like I'm not being a good enough partner. I think it probably goes back to growing up in a house where nothing was ever quite good enough, where praise was pretty rare and criticism was the default. But I'm not sure how digging into where it came from actually helps me get through this week, you know?
therapist: That's such a valid point — understanding the roots of something doesn't automatically make Tuesday night easier when you're exhausted and the kids won't sleep. What you're describing, this sense of being one mistake away from being "found out," is something we call the impostor experience, and it makes so much sense given that you grew up in an environment where the bar kept moving and approval felt out of reach. For right now, practically speaking, I'm wondering — out of everything on your plate this week, is there anything you're holding yourself to that might actually be negotiable, even just a little?

client: Maybe the house thing — like, I know rationally that if the living room is a bit messy for a few days it's not actually a crisis. But even as I say that, I feel this little spike of anxiety, like if I let that slip then it becomes two things, then three things, and suddenly everything unravels. I guess I'm not totally convinced that giving myself permission to lower the bar a little won't just turn into everything falling apart completely.
therapist: That anxiety spike makes a lot of sense — your mind is trying to protect you by treating any small slip as the top of a slippery slope, but it's worth noticing that's actually a prediction about the future, not a fact about what would really happen. In your experience, has there actually been a time when letting one small thing go led to everything genuinely falling apart, or does the catastrophe tend to stay in the "what if" space? It sounds like part of you already knows a messy living room isn't a crisis — and that part might be worth listening to a little more.

client: When I actually think about it, I can't really point to a specific time where letting something small go caused everything to completely collapse — the catastrophe does kind of stay in my head more than it happens in real life. But it's hard to trust that, because the anxiety feels so real and convincing in the moment, like my body is telling me something important even if my brain knows it's probably not rational. I guess I'm just not sure how to get those two things to line up.
therapist: You've just done something really significant — you went looking for evidence that your fear was true, and you couldn't find it, and that's worth pausing on for a moment. You're right that the anxiety feels utterly convincing in the body, and that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel* is one of the most frustrating parts of this kind of pattern — but the fact that your thinking brain and your feeling brain are starting to have that conversation is actually how they gradually begin to align. What do you think it might feel like to run a small experiment this week — letting the living room go one evening — and just notice what actually happens, rather than what the anxiety predicts?

client: I think I could maybe try that, but I'm already anticipating that I'll spend the whole evening feeling unsettled and guilty about the mess instead of actually relaxing, which kind of defeats the purpose. Like, even if nothing falls apart externally, I'm not sure my brain will let me feel okay about it in the moment. Is there something I'm supposed to do with that discomfort when it shows up, or do I just sit there feeling anxious and call it a success?
therapist: That's such a smart and honest question — you're not just agreeing to try something, you're already thinking ahead to the real obstacle, which is the discomfort itself. When the anxiety shows up, rather than trying to push it away or argue with it, you can try acknowledging it almost like a passing weather pattern — "there's that feeling again, telling me something's wrong, and I'm choosing to let the room stay messy anyway" — which is actually a form of success in itself, not just the absence of catastrophe. It's less about feeling okay in the moment and more about proving to yourself that you can tolerate the discomfort without it meaning anything has actually gone wrong — does that feel like a distinction that might make the experiment feel a little more doable?

client: That distinction actually does help a little — like, reframing it as "can I tolerate this feeling" rather than "can I make myself feel fine about it" feels more honest and maybe more achievable. But I'm a bit worried that in the moment, when I'm already tired after a full day, I won't remember to think of it that way and I'll just default back to either cleaning the room or feeling terrible about not cleaning it. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to make that reframe feel more automatic, or if it's just something that takes a lot of practice before it sticks.
therapist: You're in a really calm and reflective place right now, which is actually a great moment to do something practical — one thing that can help bridge the gap between knowing something and remembering it when you're exhausted is creating a small, concrete anchor, like a note on your phone or even just a sticky note somewhere visible that says something like "tolerating this feeling *is* the success." You're right that it takes practice before it becomes automatic, but each time you catch yourself and redirect — even imperfectly — you're actually building that new pattern, and it doesn't have to be perfect to count. What would feel like a realistic, low-pressure way to remind your future tired self of that reframe before the experiment even begins?

client: A note on my phone actually feels doable, maybe something I set as a reminder for around the time the kids go to bed when the urge to tidy up usually kicks in. I think what I'm still a little unsure about is whether one week of trying this is really going to shift something that's been wired into me for, like, thirty years — it feels like a pretty small intervention for a pretty deep pattern. But I guess I have to start somewhere, and at least this feels less abstract than some of the other things I've tried before.
therapist: You're absolutely right that one week won't rewire thirty years — and it's actually a sign of real self-awareness that you're not expecting it to, rather than setting yourself up for disappointment. What you're doing is less like flipping a switch and more like laying down the first brick of a path that gets more solid each time you choose the tolerable discomfort over the old pattern, and the fact that this feels concrete and honest to you matters more than it might seem. As you go into this week, what would feel like a meaningful enough "small win" that you'd be willing to count it as progress, even if the anxiety still shows up?

client: I think if I can leave the living room messy for even one evening and not cave and clean it up just to quiet the anxiety, I'd count that as a win — even if I feel unsettled the whole time. That feels like a low enough bar that I might actually be able to meet it without setting myself up to feel like I failed again. I'm still a little skeptical that it'll feel like progress in the moment rather than just something I white-knuckled my way through, but maybe that's okay for now.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just said — you've set a goal that's honest and achievable, and you've already given yourself permission for it to feel hard rather than easy, which is actually a much more compassionate standard than you usually hold yourself to. "White-knuckling through it" still counts, because you're not trying to feel good about the mess yet, you're just practicing the choice — and that *is* the progress, even when it doesn't feel like it in the moment. I'm glad you came today even when you weren't sure talking would help — how are you feeling about the week ahead compared to when we started?
